## Previously ...

Attribution models disagree because they are all assumptions. An experiment
replaces the assumption with evidence, and then charges you for it in sample
size.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Design an A/B test on your own site, and pre-register it
- Explain sampling variability using your own traffic volumes
- Compute the sample size a decision would require, and react honestly
- Read a test result, including a null result, without over-claiming

# 1. Why Experiments

## Selection Effects Are Large. Treatment Effects Are Small.

The most useful rule of thumb in applied marketing:

. . .

**Differences between groups of people are usually large. Differences caused by
what you did to them are usually small.**

. . .

So any comparison of two groups you did not randomise is measuring mostly
selection. The people who clicked the email differ from the people who did not,
in ways that dwarf whatever the email did.

. . .

Randomisation is the only tool that removes selection by construction rather
than by assumption.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Name the exceptions: where are treatment effects genuinely large? Price changes
and giving things away for free are two. What do they have in common?
:::

## What Randomisation Buys You

It makes the two groups **exchangeable in expectation** on everything, including
the things you did not measure and did not think of.

. . .

That is the entire trick, and nothing else in analytics does it. Every control
variable in Lecture 20's regression can only adjust for confounders you named.

. . .

**What it does not buy you**: precision. Randomisation removes bias. Sample size
removes noise. They are separate problems and a small randomised test is
unbiased and useless.

## Exogenous Variation, and Why Firms Pay For It

The reason a price experiment is worth running rather than just analysing
historical prices: **historical prices moved for reasons**.

. . .

Prices rose when demand was strong, or when costs rose, or when a competitor
exited. Regress quantity on those prices and you measure the reasons, not the
price effect. Sometimes you find that raising prices increases sales.

. . .

An experiment creates price variation that is unrelated to everything else. That
is what "exogenous" means and it is the scarce commodity.

<!-- Speaker notes: this is the cleanest available motivation for randomisation
     and it lands better than the medical framing, because they can see the
     mechanism. Keep it to five minutes; the full endogeneity treatment belongs
     in a different module. -->

## Experiments and Models Are Complements

Firms that only run experiments learn what happened at the two prices they
tested.

. . .

Firms that only model learn a lot, conditional on assumptions nobody can check.

. . .

**Together**: the experiment identifies the effect, the model extends it to
prices you did not test and to segments you could not power separately.

. . .

And the practical warning: price experiments are **visible**. Competitors,
customers, suppliers and distributors can all see them, and can all react. An
experiment is not a private act.

# 2. Design

## The One-Thing Rule

Change one thing, or you learn nothing about which thing worked.

. . .

The counter-argument is real: changing one button colour is cheap and almost
always produces a null result, because the effect is tiny relative to the noise.

. . .

**So change one thing, and make it a big one.** At portfolio volume, the only
tests worth running are tests of changes you would be nervous about.

## Hypothesis Before Data

A testable statement, with a direction, a metric, and a number, written **before
the test runs**:

> "Moving the enquiry form above the fold will increase the session-to-enquiry
> rate by at least 20% relative. Primary metric: session key event rate.
> Guardrail: bounce rate must not rise by more than 5 points."

. . .

This is the same pre-registration habit as the success statement in Lecture 2,
and it is what stops the analysis in Lecture 8 where you picked two segments
before looking.

## Choosing the Metric

**Primary metric**: one. Chosen in advance. The test succeeds or fails on it.

. . .

**Guardrail metrics**: two or three things that must not get worse. You do not
test them, you watch them.

. . .

**Everything else**: exploratory, and reported as exploratory.

. . .

Test twenty metrics and report the winner and you have not run an experiment,
you have run a search. At the conventional 5% threshold, twenty independent
metrics produce a "significant" result by chance about two thirds of the time.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
This is Lecture 8's segment-hypothesis trap in a more formal costume. Why is it
worse here than it was there?
:::

# 3. Sampling Variability

## Why Two Identical Pages Give Different Numbers

<!-- Speaker notes: this is the heart of the module's statistics content, and
     the only place students can feel it, because the n is their own. Run the
     simulation live with their real weekly traffic. Ask for predictions first,
     out loud, before running it. -->

Run the same page against itself. Split the traffic randomly. The two halves
will not report the same conversion rate.

. . .

Not because anything differs. Because 40 coin flips do not come out 20-20.

```{.python}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, p = 40, 0.05
sim = [rng.binomial(n, p)/n - rng.binomial(n, p)/n for _ in range(10000)]
np.percentile(sim, [2.5, 97.5])
```

. . .

With $n = 40$ per arm and a true 5% rate in both, the observed difference lands
anywhere within roughly ±10 percentage points. **A "doubling" is entirely
ordinary when nothing whatsoever has happened.**

## Where the Variation Comes From {.smaller}

![Source: [DS701 Tools for Data Science, Boston University](https://github.com/tools4ds/DS701-Course-Notes)](./figures/external/ds701_galton_bean_machine.png){fig-align="center" height="340px"}

*Galton's bean machine. Every bead follows the same rules and no two columns
end up the same height. That is your A/A test.*


## Confidence Intervals First

> "Between −3 and +9 percentage points."

says considerably more than

> "p = 0.31."

. . .

The interval reports **what the data can rule out**. It shows that a large
positive effect is still consistent with your result, and so is a small negative
one, which is the honest state of knowledge.

. . .

**Report the interval. Then, if you must, the p-value.**

## What a p-value Is Not

- **Not** the probability that your hypothesis is true
- **Not** the probability the result is due to chance
- **Not** a measure of effect size: a tiny effect on huge traffic gives a tiny p
- **Not** a licence to stop the test

. . .

It is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme **if nothing were
happening**. That is a narrow, conditional statement, and every over-claim in
marketing analytics comes from widening it.

## Peeking

Checking the test every day and stopping when it looks good **inflates the false
positive rate**, badly. The nominal 5% becomes 20% or worse depending on how
often you look.

. . .

The intuition: the difference wanders. Given enough looks, it will wander across
the significance threshold at some point, and you have arranged to stop
precisely then.

. . .

**Fix the duration in advance**, from the power calculation, and look at the end.
Or use a sequential testing method built for peeking, and say that you did.

## Regression to the Mean

The variant "won" in a week when the baseline was unusually bad.

. . .

Extremes are followed by less extreme values, for no reason other than that
extremes are partly luck. This is why firing the coach after a bad season
appears to work, and why the herbal remedy started after a terrible winter
appears to work.

. . .

**In marketing**: any decision triggered by an unusually bad period will look
successful. Any test started because "conversion collapsed last week" is
measuring the recovery that was coming anyway.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Does randomisation protect you from this? Both arms run in the same weeks, so
what exactly is protected, and what is not?
:::

# 4. Reality on a Small Site

## Power

To detect a 20% relative lift on a 3% base rate (3.0% versus 3.6%), at 80% power
and 5% significance, you need roughly **14,000 sessions per arm**.

. . .

Your portfolio produces perhaps 40 sessions a week.

. . .

$$\frac{2 \times 14{,}000}{40} \approx 700 \text{ weeks}$$

. . .

**Thirteen years.** Compute it live with the room's actual traffic. The answer is
uncomfortable and the discomfort is the lesson.

## What to Do Instead

1. **Test bigger changes.** Effect size is in the numerator. A whole new landing
   page can move a rate by 50%; a button colour cannot
2. **Move up the funnel.** Click-through on a link happens 30 times more often
   than an enquiry. Test on the frequent event, and be explicit that it is a
   proxy
3. **Run longer, and accept the seasonality** you have bought
4. **Change the question.** Five user interviews will tell you more about your
   enquiry form than an underpowered A/B test, and you can say why

. . .

**Or run it and report the interval.** An honest wide interval is a legitimate
deliverable in this module.

## Reporting a Null Result

"No detectable difference, 95% CI −4 to +6 points, n = 380 per arm" is a
**finding**. It says the effect, if any, is not large.

. . .

"The variant won, 8% versus 5%" on n = 30 is not a finding. It is a coin flip
with a conclusion attached.

. . .

**Documented judgement beats undocumented certainty.** The marking here rewards
the student who computed the power, found it impossible, ran the test anyway and
reported honestly, over the one who declared a winner.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

On your own portfolio:

1. Write a hypothesis with a direction, a primary metric and a guardrail
2. Compute the sample size needed for a 20% relative lift on your base rate
3. Compare it to your actual weekly traffic and state how long the test would
   take
4. Decide what you will do about that, and write the decision down
5. Run the test anyway, and report the confidence interval rather than a winner

**30 minutes**

# 5. AI and the Temptation to Over-Claim

## AI This Block: An analyst you interrogate

Where we are on the module's AI spine, introduced in Lecture 10:

> **An analyst you interrogate**

## It Will Not Stop You

<!-- Speaker notes: run this live. Give an assistant a fake result on n=30 and
     watch it write a confident, well-structured recommendation with next steps.
     It is the most persuasive demonstration in the whole module. Then run the
     fixed prompt on the same numbers. -->

> "Variant B converted at 8% versus 5% for A, 30 sessions each. What should I
> do?"

. . .

You will get a recommendation. Probably a well-organised one, with next steps and
a note about continuing to monitor.

. . .

It will rarely volunteer, unprompted, that 30 sessions cannot support any
conclusion at all.

## The Prompt That Fixes It

> "Before recommending anything, compute the confidence interval for the
> difference in proportions, state the minimum detectable effect at this sample
> size, and tell me whether this sample can support a conclusion."

. . .

Same numbers, entirely different answer.

. . .

**The obligation to ask is yours.** That is the single sentence to take out of
this lecture, and it generalises well past A/B tests.

## Using It Properly {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Reliable**

- Power and sample-size calculations
- Simulation code for the peeking demonstration
- Explaining what a confidence interval means, in client language
- Listing the guardrail metrics you forgot
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Never**

- Deciding whether to stop the test
- Judging whether the effect is practically important
- Telling you whether the randomisation actually worked
- Choosing the primary metric after seeing the data
:::
::::

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Give an assistant your real test result and ask for a recommendation
2. Then ask for the confidence interval and the minimum detectable effect
3. Compare the two answers and write what changed
4. Ask it to compute your required sample size, and check its arithmetic against
   an online calculator

**15 minutes**
